title: Parametric types and generic numerical code
outcome: Express useful type relationships without confusing subtype relations, storage representation or a method signature.
key_terms: A type with parameters, such as `Point{T}`, where each concrete instance like `Point{Float64}` is a distinct type.
Syntax such as `where {T<:Real}` that introduces a type variable and bounds the types a method accepts.
A `Vector{Float64}` is not a subtype of `Vector{Real}`, even though `Float64` is a subtype of `Real`.
The supertype of vectors, ranges and views, so methods annotated with it accept more containers than `Vector` does.
A function is type stable when its argument types determine one concrete return type, which lets the compiler specialize it.
approach: `typed_total` is parametric in `T<:Real` and starts from `zero(T)`, so integers, rationals, `Float32` and `BigInt` keep their own representation. Parametric containers are invariant, so `Vector{Float64}` is not a `Vector{Real}`; the signature `AbstractVector{<:Real}` expresses the intended family instead.

exercises.title: Preserve a rational
exercises.hint: Use a compatible zero and arithmetic.
exercises.answer: A hardcoded floating accumulator would change the representation contract.
exercises.why: With `T = Rational{Int}`, the accumulator starts at `0//1` and adds 1//3 and 2//3 exactly to get `1//1`.
exercises.wrong: Initializing `total = 0.0` converts the sum to `Float64`, so the result is approximately 1.0 and no longer rational.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `typed_total([1//3, 2//3]) == 1//1`; also check `typeof` of the result is `Rational{Int}`.

exercises.title: Handle an empty concrete vector
exercises.answer: This empty-input policy is valid for this additive operation, not every statistic.
exercises.why: `Int[]` still has element type `Int`, so `zero(Int)` is returned without the loop running, giving 0.
exercises.wrong: Using `values[1]` as the initial total fails on an empty vector, and applying the same identity idea to a mean would be wrong.

exercises.title: Inspect invariance
exercises.task: Test whether Vector{Float64} is a subtype of Vector{Real}.
exercises.hint: Compare exact container parameters with a family constraint.
exercises.answer: The two vector types have different representation and mutation contracts.
exercises.why: Invariance means `Vector{Float64} <: Vector{Real}` is false, since a `Vector{Real}` could store any real and a `Float64` vector cannot.
exercises.wrong: Assuming covariance, as with Python type hints for read-only sequences, predicts true and leads to signatures that reject float vectors.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `!(Vector{Float64} <: Vector{Real})` and `Vector{Float64} <: AbstractVector{<:Real}`.

exercises.title: Accept a useful family
exercises.task: Use AbstractVector{<:Real} in a method signature.
exercises.expected: Concrete real vectors can be accepted.
exercises.hint: Express the intended family without forcing a conversion.
exercises.answer: A suitable signature can preserve generic behavior and avoid unnecessary restrictions.
exercises.why: `accepts_reals(values::AbstractVector{<:Real})` accepts `[1//2]` because `Rational{Int}` is a subtype of `Real`, returning its length 1.
exercises.wrong: Annotating the parameter as `Vector{Real}` rejects nearly all concrete vectors, forcing callers to convert data first.

exercises.title: Reject unrelated elements
exercises.task: Pass a vector of strings to the real-vector method.
exercises.hint: The domain constraint is meaningful here.
exercises.answer: Broadening a signature requires defining the corresponding arithmetic or behavior.
exercises.why: `String` is not a subtype of `Real`, so no method matches a string vector and Julia raises `MethodError`.
exercises.wrong: Widening the signature to `AbstractVector` makes the call succeed until `+` or `zero` fails deeper inside.

exercises.title: Connect to differentiation
exercises.task: Explain why an output buffer should not always be Float64.
exercises.expected: It may discard or reject another numeric representation.
exercises.hint: Type relationships can carry derivative information.
exercises.answer: Generic arithmetic is needed for methods such as forward-mode differentiation, subject to their own supported-operation contract.
exercises.why: Forward-mode automatic differentiation passes dual numbers through the same arithmetic, and a `zeros(Float64, n)` buffer cannot hold them.
exercises.wrong: Hardcoding `Float64` output storage either throws on dual inputs or strips their derivative part, making the gradient wrong or absent.
exercises.verify: Show `typed_total(Float32[1, 2]) isa Float32` and `typed_total(BigInt[1, 2]) == 3` from the reference as evidence that generic code preserves type.

checks_note: `typed_total(Float32[1, 2]) isa Float32` shows that starting from `zero(eltype(values))` keeps the element type, and the `BigInt` case shows the same code serving arbitrary precision. `accepts_reals` takes a rational and rejects text by dispatch, because `String` is not a `Real`. The two concreteness lines separate an abstract container type, `AbstractVector{Float64}`, which suits signatures, from `Vector{Float64}`, which suits stored fields. Together these lines cover the three questions the lesson asks of every signature: what result type comes back, which argument types are accepted, and which are refused before any work starts. A version that started the total at the integer literal 0 would return `Float64` for `Float32` input after promotion, or keep `Int` where a `BigInt` sum was needed.
